596.title: All scripture (2 Timothy 3:14–17)
596.hook: scripture is inspired and useful for teaching and correcting (CCC 105)
596.howItsDone: Catholics hear Scripture at every Mass and many practice lectio divina, slow prayerful reading; the Church teaches that Scripture is inspired by God and is read within the living Tradition of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, coals under the ash, and a gift fanned back into flame. Your line was stir up the gift. Which gift did you use? Day five hundred ninety-six.

Hold your hand in front of your mouth and breathe out slowly. You feel it: warm, moving, alive. The word inspire comes from the Latin for breathing in. Today's word, inspiration, describes what Christians believe about the Bible. And it comes from a single Greek word that appears exactly once in the whole Bible, near the end of the second letter to Timothy. Paul is reminding his young friend of the scriptures he's known since he was a child.
screen: `BREATHE ON YOUR HAND.` → `INSPIRE: TO BREATHE IN.` → `A WORD USED EXACTLY ONCE.`

segments.voice: From infancy, Paul says, you have known the holy scriptures. For Timothy, that meant the Jewish scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament; the New was still being written. Then: "All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice, That the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work." Inspired of God is one Greek word: theopneustos. Theos, God. Pneō, to breathe. God-breathed. It may remind a reader of Genesis, where God breathes into the first man and he becomes a living soul. The words on the page carry God's breath. Then four uses. To teach and to reprove are about what to believe. To correct and to instruct in justice are about how to live. Scripture, here, isn't a museum piece. It's a working tool, so the person of God is equipped for every good work. What do Catholics mean by inspiration? The Catechism says God is the author of Sacred Scripture. But the Second Vatican Council adds something important: the human writers were true authors too. God chose them and used them with their own powers and abilities, their language, their style, their era. So you can hear Paul's temper and Luke's careful research and the psalmist's grief, and still say the words are God's. The Council says the books teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wanted put into writing for the sake of our salvation. And it says Scripture must be read in the same Spirit in which it was written. For Catholics, that means reading it within the Church, together with Tradition. Breathed out once. Breathed in every time it's read.
screen: `TIMOTHY'S SCRIPTURES.` · `THEOPNEUSTOS: GOD-BREATHED.` · `TEACH, REPROVE, CORRECT, INSTRUCT.` · `GOD AND HUMAN AUTHORS, BOTH TRUE.` · then, large: `ALL SCRIPTURE, INSPIRED OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse slowly. Choose any verse you know, or use today's: all scripture, inspired of God. Settle, and breathe. Say it once, slowly, in your head. Then again, and notice which word stands out. Then a third time, and stay with that one word. Let it rise and fall with your breath, breathed in, breathed out. Don't analyze it. Just let it be read. If you pray, you can answer the word with a word of your own. If you don't, simply notice what one slow verse does to the next minute. The bell holds the time.
Inspiration. From the Greek theopneustos, God-breathed: Catholics believe Scripture has God as its author, written through true human authors. Today's word.

597.title: I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:6–8)
597.hook: Paul near the end: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course
597.tomorrow: Let no man despise thy youth
597.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome pray at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, built over the place tradition names as his tomb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all scripture, inspired of God. Your line was god-breathed. Which word stood out when you read your verse three times? Day five hundred ninety-seven.

Tradition says Paul was beheaded outside the walls of Rome, near the road to Ostia, under the emperor Nero. Pilgrims still visit a great basilica built over the place tradition names as his tomb, Saint Paul Outside the Walls. In 2009, Pope Benedict the Sixteenth announced that tiny fragments of bone inside the old sarcophagus there had been dated to the first or second century. Second Timothy presents itself as Paul's last letter, written in chains, knowing what was coming. Today, his farewell.
screen: `OUTSIDE THE WALLS OF ROME.` → `A TOMB AND A BASILICA.` → `A FAREWELL IN CHAINS.`

segments.voice: "For I am even now ready to be sacrificed: and the time of my dissolution is at hand." Ready to be sacrificed is one Greek word, spendomai: to be poured out, like wine poured over an altar as an offering. Paul sees his death that way. Not taken from him. Poured out. And the Greek word behind dissolution is analysis, a loosening: a ship slipping its moorings, soldiers striking their tents to move on. Then the sentence people carve on gravestones: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Three pictures. An athlete or a soldier who stayed in the fight. A runner who reached the line; remember Paul pressing toward the mark in Philippians. And a guard who kept what was entrusted to him, all the way to the end, and handed it on intact. Then he looks ahead to a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will give him, and not only him, but all who love his coming. And then, right after the most famous lines, something wonderfully ordinary. Bring my cloak that I left at Troas, he asks Timothy, and the books, especially the parchments. Only Luke is with me. Come before winter. A man near death, cold, a little lonely, wanting a coat and something to read. The farewell doesn't make him a statue. Catholics celebrate Paul with Peter every year on June twenty-ninth, the two apostles Rome remembers as martyrs. Kept the faith doesn't mean a spotless record. Paul never hid that he had once hunted down Christians; he called himself the least of the apostles because of it. It means he didn't put the faith down.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one course. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you started and left unfinished. A letter. A book. A repair. An apology. A promise to visit. Choose one that you could actually finish, or take one real step on, today. Picture the finish line: the last sentence written, the last page turned, the door knocked on. Notice how it would feel to be done. If you pray, you can ask for the strength to finish it. If you don't, simply set the time when you'll do it. The bell holds the time.

598.title: Let no man despise thy youth (1 Timothy 4:12)
598.word: Let no man despise thy youth
598.hook: be an example in word, conduct, charity, faith
598.howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds World Youth Day gatherings, and Pope Francis addressed young people directly in the 2019 apostolic exhortation Christus Vivit; young saints such as Carlo Acutis are held up as examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farewell in chains: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course. Your line was I have kept the faith. What did you finish? Day five hundred ninety-eight.

Most people have been the youngest one in the room at least once. The meeting where nobody quite looks at you when you speak. The family dinner where your opinion gets a pat on the head. Timothy knew that room. Paul had left him in charge of the church at Ephesus, with older members who could remember things he couldn't. We don't know exactly how old Timothy was. In that world, young could mean anyone under forty. Paul's first letter to him has a line for exactly this.
screen: `THE YOUNGEST ONE IN THE ROOM.` → `TIMOTHY, LEFT IN CHARGE.` → `A LINE FOR EXACTLY THIS.`

segments.voice: "Let no man despise thy youth: but be thou an example of the faithful in word, in conversation, in charity, in faith, in chastity." Look at what Paul doesn't say. He doesn't say demand respect. He doesn't say pull rank, or remind them who appointed you. He says: be an example. Earn it by how you live. Then he names five places to be seen. In word: how you speak. In conversation, which in old English means not talk but conduct, your whole way of life. In charity. In faith. In chastity, a clean heart. Then the habits that support it: attend to reading, to exhortation, to teaching. Don't neglect the grace that was given you with the laying on of hands. Meditate on these things, be wholly in them, so that your progress may be seen by all. Notice the last bit: progress. Paul doesn't expect Timothy to be finished. He expects him to be visibly growing. The Catholic Church has spent a good deal of attention on young people in recent years. In 2019, Pope Francis wrote a whole letter to the young, called Christ Is Alive, insisting they are not only the future of the Church but its present. And in 2025 the Church canonized Carlo Acutis, an Italian teenager who loved computers and the Eucharist and died of leukemia at fifteen. The Church now calls him a saint. Paul's advice cuts both ways. To the young, it says: be an example. To everyone else, it says the same thing as its first words. Don't despise them.
screen: `NOT 'DEMAND RESPECT': BE AN EXAMPLE.` · `CONVERSATION: YOUR WHOLE CONDUCT.` · `PROGRESS THAT CAN BE SEEN.` · `A SAINT WHO DIED AT FIFTEEN.` · then, large: `LET NO MAN DESPISE THY YOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture one young person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone younger than you: a child, a teenager, a new coworker, a niece, a student. Picture their face. Think of one real thing they do well, something you've actually seen, not a general compliment. Hold it. Think how you might tell them, in a sentence, today. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care, and keep hold of the sentence. The bell holds the time.

599.title: Philemon
599.hook: Paul sends a runaway slave back as a beloved brother; Christians later drew on this against slavery, too slowly
599.howItsDone: The Catholic Church today condemns slavery as an offense against human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; Catechism 2414), and remembers Philemon and Onesimus in its readings and saints' calendars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, let no man despise thy youth: be an example. Your line was be an example. Who did you tell what they do well? Day five hundred ninety-nine.

It's the shortest of Paul's letters, twenty-five verses, and it's about one man. His name was Onesimus. He was enslaved in the household of a Christian named Philemon. At some point he left, whether he ran away or went looking for Paul's help, the letter doesn't say. He ended up with Paul, who was in prison, and there he became a Christian. Now Paul is sending him back. And he sends him with this letter in his hand.
screen: `TWENTY-FIVE VERSES, ONE MAN.` → `ONESIMUS LEAVES PHILEMON.` → `PAUL SENDS HIM BACK, WITH A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Paul could give orders, he says, but he'd rather ask. "I beseech thee for my son, whom I have begotten in my bands, Onesimus, Who hath been heretofore unprofitable to thee, but now is profitable both to me and thee." That's a pun. Onesimus means useful. Once useless to you, now useful. Then the heart of the letter: receive him "not now as a servant, but instead of a servant, a most dear brother." A brother, in the flesh and in the Lord. Then Paul puts his own name on the line: if he owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write it with my own hand. I will repay it. Now the hard part, said plainly. Paul never commands Philemon to set Onesimus free. He says he's confident Philemon will do even more than he asks, and readers have argued ever since about whether that's a hint. We don't know what Philemon did. And this little letter was later used on both sides. Some slaveholders, including in the American South, cited it to defend returning people who had escaped. Others pointed to its words, no longer a servant but a brother, against slavery itself. Christians, the Catholic Church among them, came to condemn slavery far too slowly. Popes condemned the slave trade in the nineteenth century, and the Second Vatican Council listed slavery among the things that poison human society and insult the Creator. Around the year 110, Ignatius of Antioch wrote of a bishop of Ephesus named Onesimus. Some think it was the same man. Nobody can be sure.
screen: `ONESIMUS: 'USEFUL'.` · `NOT A SERVANT: A MOST DEAR BROTHER.` · `CHARGE IT TO MY ACCOUNT.` · `A LETTER USED ON BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `NOT NOW AS A SERVANT, BUT A MOST DEAR BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about who you call brother. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you'd call brother or sister without thinking: family, close friends. Now widen the circle. Think of someone who serves you and whose name you don't know: a cleaner, a driver, a cashier, someone who picks the fruit you eat. Picture them as clearly as you can. Let the word brother or sister sit next to them. Notice what changes. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them in that word. The bell holds the time.
Philemon. Paul's shortest letter: sending Onesimus back, not as a servant, but as a most dear brother. Today's word.

600.title: Sharper than a sword (Hebrews 4:12)
600.hook: the word of God is living and effectual
600.howItsDone: At Mass the Book of the Gospels may be carried in the entrance procession, placed on the altar, incensed and kissed before the Gospel is proclaimed; Catholics stand to hear the Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philemon, and a slave sent back as a brother. Your line was no longer a servant. Whose name did you learn? Day six hundred.

Nobody knows who wrote the letter to the Hebrews. It names no author. Early Christians guessed Paul, or Barnabas, or Apollos, or Luke. In the third century the great scholar Origen said, more or less, that only God knows. It reads less like a letter than a sermon, written for Christians who were tired and tempted to drift away. Today begins its stretch, Hebrews and James. And the preacher of Hebrews has a lot to say about how God speaks.
screen: `NO NAME ON THE LETTER.` → `ONLY GOD KNOWS WHO WROTE IT.` → `A SERMON FOR THE TIRED.`

segments.voice: He's just been quoting a psalm: today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts. Today. The psalm was centuries old, and he treats it as spoken right now, to his listeners. That's the setup for today's verse: "For the word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two edged sword; and reaching unto the division of the soul and the spirit, of the joints also and the marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." Living: not a fossil. Effectual is the Greek energēs, where English gets energy: it works, it does things. And then the sword. Not a soldier's long blade, but a short, sharp one, and look at what it cuts. Soul from spirit. Joints from marrow. That's not a battlefield. That's surgery. The picture is closer to a scalpel than a weapon: something that reaches the places you can't reach yourself and shows what's actually there. Discerner, in Greek, is kritikos, where English gets critic. The word of God reads you while you read it. The next verse says it plainly: nothing is hidden from his sight, everything is naked and open to his eyes. That could sound frightening. The preacher means it as the start of healing: you can't treat what you can't see. Catholics honor the word with their bodies. At Mass the Book of the Gospels can be carried in procession, held high, incensed and kissed. The Second Vatican Council said the Church has always venerated the Scriptures just as it venerates the Lord's body, and that in them the Father meets his children and speaks with them.
screen: `TODAY, IF YOU HEAR HIS VOICE.` · `LIVING AND EFFECTUAL: ENERGĒS.` · `A SCALPEL MORE THAN A WEAPON.` · `IT READS YOU WHILE YOU READ IT.` · then, large: `THE WORD OF GOD IS LIVING AND EFFECTUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one verse cut through. Choose a verse that has ever unsettled you, or use today's: the word of God is living and effectual. Settle, and breathe. Say it slowly, once. Don't argue with it, and don't defend yourself. Just notice where it lands. Which part of you does it touch? A worry, a habit, an old wound? Stay there. If you pray, you can ask God to show you what's there, and to heal it. If you don't, simply notice what the words uncovered, without judging it. The bell holds the time.
Sharper than a sword. Hebrews' picture of God's word: living, at work, reaching where nothing else reaches, and reading the heart. Today's word.
Your line: living and effectual. Today, read one line of Scripture before you read anything else, and notice what it touches. Day six hundred.

601.title: One who has compassion (Hebrews 4:14–16)
601.hook: a high priest tempted in all things like us, without sin
601.tomorrow: The substance of things hoped for
601.howItsDone: Catholics bring their weaknesses to Christ in personal prayer, in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, and in the sacrament of penance, where they believe Christ forgives through the priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word of God, sharper than a two-edged sword. Your line was living and effectual. Where did your verse land? Day six hundred one.

When you're scared before an operation, a nurse who once had the same surgery says something different from one who hasn't. Same words, maybe: it'll be okay. But you hear them differently, because she's been there. Hebrews builds its whole argument around a picture from Israel's worship: the high priest, who once a year on the Day of Atonement entered the holiest place to seek mercy for the people. And today the preacher says something surprising about the high priest Christians have.
screen: `A NURSE WHO'S BEEN THERE.` → `THE HIGH PRIEST, ONCE A YEAR.` → `A HIGH PRIEST WHO UNDERSTANDS.`

segments.voice: First he says who it is: a great high priest who has passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, so hold fast to what you profess. Then the surprise: "For we have not a high priest, who can not have compassion on our infirmities: but one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin." The Greek word for have compassion is sympathēsai, where English gets sympathy: to suffer with, to feel alongside. Not pity from above. Fellow feeling from inside. Tempted in all things like as we are. Hebrews means it. A chapter later it says that in the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications with a strong cry and tears. The Gospels show him hungry in the desert, tempted there, exhausted, grieving at a friend's tomb, in anguish in Gethsemane. And yet without sin. Catholic teaching holds both together. The Council of Chalcedon said he is like us in all things but sin. Sinlessness, in this picture, doesn't make him distant from the tempted. Many Christian writers have argued that one who never gave way under temptation felt its full weight, and so knows its full strength. Then the invitation: "Let us go therefore with confidence to the throne of grace: that we may obtain mercy, and find grace in seasonable aid." With confidence. The Greek word means boldness, the freedom to speak openly. Seasonable aid means help at the right moment, when you need it. Catholics hear this invitation in many places: in personal prayer, before the tabernacle, and in confession, where they believe Christ's mercy meets them through the priest. He understands. That's the whole of today's line.
screen: `A GREAT HIGH PRIEST.` · `SYMPATHY: TO SUFFER WITH.` · `TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS, WITHOUT SIN.` · `GO WITH CONFIDENCE.` · then, large: `ONE TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS LIKE AS WE ARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one weakness. Settle, and breathe. Think of one weakness you're ashamed of, the kind you'd rather nobody saw. A temptation that keeps winning. A fear. A failure you keep repeating. Don't hide it, and don't beat yourself up about it either. Just hold it up, honestly. If you pray, you can bring it to Christ as Hebrews invites: with confidence, to someone who understands. If you don't, simply picture telling it to someone who has been exactly there, and notice what that feels like. The bell holds the time.
One who has compassion. Hebrews' picture of Jesus as high priest: tempted in all things like us, without sin, and able to suffer with us. Today's word.

602.title: The substance of things hoped for (Hebrews 11)
602.hook: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sara and the long list of the faithful
602.howItsDone: Catholics hear parts of Hebrews 11 in the Sunday and weekday readings at Mass, and the chapter's list of the faithful is often read alongside the Church's teaching on the communion of saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the high priest tempted in all things like us: one who has compassion. Your line was he understands. What weakness did you bring him? Day six hundred two.

Many families keep a list like this somewhere. Names written inside the cover of an old Bible. Photos stuck to a fridge. A grandmother who prayed through a war. An uncle who started over in a new country with one suitcase. Nobody on the list is perfect, and all of them kept walking toward something they couldn't see yet. Hebrews eleven is that list for the whole Church. The writer has spent ten chapters on Christ the high priest. Then, before the hard advice of chapter twelve, he stops and reads out the family names. And he opens with a definition.
screen: `NAMES INSIDE AN OLD BIBLE.` → `HEBREWS READS THE FAMILY LIST.` → `IT OPENS WITH A DEFINITION.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims gives it like this: "Now faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not." Two halves. Substance first. The Greek word is hypostasis, literally what stands underneath: a foundation, the thing that holds something up. In this line faith isn't a mood or a guess. It's the ground under a hope, giving it somewhere to stand before it arrives. Then evidence: a conviction about what can't be seen yet. Then the names, one after another, each opening the same way: by faith. By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain. Noah built an ark for a flood nobody had ever seen. Abraham "went out, not knowing whither he went." Sara, long past the age for children, received strength to conceive, because she believed that the one who promised was faithful. Then Moses, Rahab, and a rush of names the writer says there isn't time to finish: Gideon, Samson, David, Samuel, the prophets. Here's the surprise. The chapter says plainly that these people died without receiving what was promised. They saw it from far off and greeted it, like travelers waving at a city on the horizon. And the last verse says they would not be made perfect without us. The list isn't closed. It's waiting for more names. Catholics hear the communion of saints in this: the faithful who have gone before are still one family with the living. The next chapter calls them a cloud of witnesses, surrounding the race.
screen: `HYPOSTASIS: WHAT STANDS UNDERNEATH.` · `BY FAITH: ABEL, NOAH, ABRAHAM, SARA.` · `THEY DIED WITHOUT RECEIVING IT.` · `NOT MADE PERFECT WITHOUT US.` · then, large: `FAITH IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THINGS TO BE HOPED FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add a name to the list. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind someone whose faith held you up, alive or gone: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who kept going through something hard. Say their name quietly. Then finish the line the way Hebrews does: by faith, they... Let the sentence end however it ends. Kept a promise. Got up early to pray. Forgave. Stay with them a while. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, just hold the name with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Faith. In Hebrews eleven, the substance of things hoped for: the ground a hope stands on before it arrives. Today's word.

Your line: faith is the substance. Today, tell the person whose name you added, or someone who knew them, what they gave you. And that's week eighty-six: god-breathed, I have kept the faith, be an example, Philemon, sharper than a sword, he understands, and faith. Day six hundred two.
